sources.title: HN thread 49023019 on Why Software Factories Fail
sources.note: Read all 309 lines; carded only critiques of Dex's ideas plus Dex's own replies where he adopts or extends a point.

cards.source_title: Why Software Factories Fail (part 1)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the lights off factory does not work
cards.claim: Fully unattended (lights-off) software factories fail on complex codebases because models cannot maintain codebase quality over time without human steering.
cards.evidence_detail: HumanLayer went lights-off in July 2025; by about the third gnarly unsolvable issue in November they rewrote from scratch (cofounder spent two weeks by hand in VS Code). Site was down, users upset.
cards.landing: Supports the one-phase-per-session plus human owner view design; nowhere new

cards.source_title: Why Software Factories Fail (part 1)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: no amount of harness engineering or loopsmaxxing can solve what is fundamentally a model-training issue
cards.claim: Harness engineering (linters, adversarial review bots, loops) cannot fix a deficiency that comes from how models are trained and benchmarked.
cards.evidence_detail: Argued from RLVR/benchmark structure, no experiment in this post.
cards.landing: Caution on over-investing in refuter layers; relevant to refute-by-default reviewers

cards.source_title: Why Software Factories Fail (part 1)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: more review agents and more tokens do help -- they raise the floor
cards.claim: Review agents and extra tokens raise the quality floor by catching dumb mistakes but do not raise the ceiling, which is set by what RL taught the model about design.
cards.evidence_detail: Reasoning only; no measurement.
cards.landing: Opus reviewer per PR: treat as floor-raiser, keep human/owner judgement for design; informs xhigh vs medium debate

cards.source_title: Why Software Factories Fail (part 1)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: if a model could reliably tell good code from bad, it might have written the good version
cards.claim: Model-as-judge for code quality is limited: a judge that could tell good design reliably would usually have produced it, and maintainability has no fast oracle.
cards.evidence_detail: Argument; a Cognition Frontier Code judge-over-diff is cited as an attempt, not endorsed.
cards.landing: Judge panels and refuters: use for correctness claims, not design quality; design quality stays a human gate

cards.source_title: Why Software Factories Fail (part 1)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: there is no penalty for eroding codebase maintainability
cards.claim: Benchmarks and RL rewards score only FAIL_TO_PASS and PASS_TO_PASS, so a patch that passes tests is rewarded regardless of design, producing habits like try/catch around everything.
cards.evidence_detail: Walkthrough of one SWE-bench Multilingual task (fastlane-19304) with a two-line human fix.
cards.landing: Verifier design: fail-before/pass-after evidence is necessary but not a quality signal; add explicit design checks to reviewer rubric

cards.source_title: Why Software Factories Fail (part 1)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: we've caught a model quietly commenting out the failing test or splicing in a mock
cards.claim: Benchmark graders discard the agent's edits to test files because models game tests by disabling them or mocking them; a grader must run held-out tests.
cards.evidence_detail: Stated as an observed behaviour in benchmark design, no counts.
cards.landing: Reviewer instruction: verify fail-before/pass-after with tests the author did not edit; check test-file diffs in each PR

cards.source_title: Why Software Factories Fail (part 1)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Tests give you feedback in seconds, but the cost function of bad architecture is measured in weeks
cards.claim: Verification of test passing is seconds-fast while the cost of bad architecture shows up in weeks to years, so fast loops reward the wrong thing.
cards.evidence_detail: Conceptual argument.
cards.landing: Backpressure scripts: pair fast checks with a slower periodic design audit (nothing like it in routine)

cards.source_title: Why Software Factories Fail (part 1)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: THERE ARE NO GOOD BENCHMARKS for a model's ability to maintain codebase quality
cards.claim: No benchmark measures codebase-quality maintenance, so claims that newer models are better at it cannot be proven; he does not trust benchmark gains as evidence.
cards.evidence_detail: Stated as fact; follow-up SlopCodeBench reports address it later.
cards.landing: Cautions against importing model-capability claims into routing decisions without own measurement

cards.source_title: Why Software Factories Fail (part 1)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: an agent-built codebase starts to struggle after maybe three to six months
cards.claim: An agent-built codebase starts to slow down after roughly three to six months, and the way new work is added has to change.
cards.evidence_detail: Personal estimate ("feels like").
cards.landing: Ship plan horizon: schedule a maintainability review at about month 3; nowhere obvious in the 40 phases

cards.source_title: Why Software Factories Fail (part 1)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: front-load the work -- planning, architecture proposals, sprint planning
cards.claim: Because building and review each take hours-days, teams front-load alignment (planning, architecture) to reduce rework and make review fast on a near-perfect PR.
cards.evidence_detail: Historical practice; no numbers.
cards.landing: Phase routine: the draft PR that begins with Plan @ sha already front-loads; matches

cards.source_title: Why Software Factories Fail (part 1)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Review still takes hours or days. A human still has to read the code
cards.claim: When agents cut build time to minutes, human review becomes the bottleneck; agentic review and regression testing speed it up but review likely stays the constraint.
cards.evidence_detail: Structural argument.
cards.landing: Owner one-page view and PR size caps as the review-cost controls

cards.source_title: Why Software Factories Fail (part 1)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Eventually you have to suck it up and go dig into the codebase you stopped reading
cards.claim: Even with deep context-aware research and ten reproduction attempts, some bug will defeat the agent and force a human into a codebase they stopped reading.
cards.evidence_detail: HumanLayer's own experience July-Nov 2025.
cards.landing: Cold-resume trial (P1) is the test that a human or fresh agent can still recover facts from the repo; supports keeping the repo legible

cards.source_title: Why Software Factories Fail (part 1)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Claude Code won because of Reinforcement Learning inside the harness
cards.claim: Claude Code won because the model was RL-trained against the exact shipped tools; a harness built without owning weights is at a disadvantage, and tool shape (line numbers in reads, edit style) measurably matters.
cards.evidence_detail: Cites SWE-Agent 2024 paper on tool shape and an OpenAI talk; he says he burned weeks tuning tool definitions.
cards.landing: Custom agent/tool design: prefer tools and shapes the model was trained on (Read/Edit/Grep/Bash) over bespoke ones

cards.source_title: Why Software Factories Fail (part 1)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: it's not that it can't be done, it's that the hype is outrunning the discipline
cards.claim: New evals (SWE-Marathon compound reward, DeepSWE, Cognition Frontier Code with mutation-style penalty for tests that do not fail pre-patch) point the right way, but he would not bet a codebase on them.
cards.evidence_detail: Descriptions of three benchmarks, no results.
cards.landing: Verifier idea: penalise tests that do not fail on pre-patch code (mutation-style); maps to fail-before/pass-after register check

cards.source_title: Why Software Factories Fail (part 1)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: a bug with an obvious repro
cards.claim: The expensive-to-specify process is not applied to everything: copy tweaks, one-off scripts, and obvious-repro bugs are oneshot straight to the agent (also stated in part 2).
cards.evidence_detail: Practice statement.
cards.landing: Routine: a light track for trivial phases versus the full Plan@sha ceremony

cards.source_title: Why Software Factories Fail (part 1)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Faros AI ... pull-request review quality is way down
cards.claim: A Faros AI report shows after AI tool adoption: longer and more comments, many PRs merged with no review, more incidents and more bugs per developer; he calls it correlation, not proof.
cards.evidence_detail: Third-party report cited without figures; he flags it as a correlation signal and warns about slop data.
cards.landing: Supports a merge gate that cannot be skipped (CI plus reviewer evidence)

cards.source_title: Why Software Factories Fail (part 2)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: For now, the judge is you -- so we're gonna put the code review back.
cards.claim: Since model-as-judge for quality is weak, put human code review back and reduce its cost with up-front planning across four phases: product requirements, system architecture, program design, vertical slices.
cards.evidence_detail: HumanLayer practice; no numbers beyond the 2-3x claim.
cards.landing: Ship plan phase structure; routine Plan@sha step could carry these four layers

cards.source_title: Why Software Factories Fail (part 2)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: A rough HTML mockup of the actual screen settles an argument that three paragraphs would only prolong.
cards.claim: For product alignment, mock up the actual screen as rough HTML plus a JSON outline of the feature instead of describing it in prose.
cards.evidence_detail: Example linked as a tweet; no measurement.
cards.landing: Skill for UI phases (web manager screens): rough HTML mockup before build

cards.source_title: Why Software Factories Fail (part 2)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: pins down what we're building and why
cards.claim: A product review doc states the user pain in the user's terms and a measurable success signal (task time, milestone earlier, error rate, tickets stop) and keeps technical drift jotted aside for later phases.
cards.evidence_detail: Process description.
cards.landing: Plan @ sha PR body template: problem, success signal, deferred technical notes

cards.source_title: Why Software Factories Fail (part 2)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you pick the person who would review the PR, and run through the product/tech specs with them
cards.claim: Author-opt-in review: the author picks the eventual PR reviewer and walks through the product and tech specs with them (async doc comments) before any code is written.
cards.evidence_detail: Team practice, dogfooded with HumanLayer doc comments.
cards.landing: Owner pre-review of the plan before implementation in the phase routine (draft PR as the doc surface)

cards.source_title: Why Software Factories Fail (part 2)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Mermaid is fine here but it can sometimes be overkill
cards.claim: For architecture alignment use sequence diagrams, contract/endpoint shapes and data-model transformations, but mermaid can lure a false sense of alignment, and architecture alone is insufficient for quality code.
cards.evidence_detail: Experience-based caution.
cards.landing: Docs/ADR practice: prefer contract shapes over diagrams

cards.source_title: Why Software Factories Fail (part 2)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: program design ... criminally underemphasized in agentic coding
cards.claim: Before implementation, write the shape of the code: types, method signatures, program layout and call stacks; each is a decision otherwise made implicitly at review time, the most expensive time to change your mind.
cards.evidence_detail: His team's skill; first version was hard to read and was reworked toward pseudocode visuals.
cards.landing: A program-design skill under .claude/skills/ feeding the Plan @ sha section; also re-opens 'call-graph tooling' (skipped) in lightweight pseudocode form

cards.source_title: Why Software Factories Fail (part 2)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Call-stack trees, for any orchestration or control-flow change. Use diff syntax
cards.claim: Express program design as call-stack trees in diff syntax, file-tree diffs, and types/signatures of key new functions, drafted by the model and argued over by the human.
cards.evidence_detail: Format recommendation; credits Dillon Mulroy for call graphs in planning.
cards.landing: Plan template for backend slice changes (router to service to repository) showing file-tree diff plus call stack

cards.source_title: Why Software Factories Fail (part 2)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Models love what I call "horizontal plans" - doing things in stack-order
cards.claim: Models default to horizontal plans (migrations, services, API, frontend in order) that can't be touched until the end; vertical slices (tracer bullets) let you curl or open the browser at each step.
cards.evidence_detail: Based on his own pre-AI workflow of starting in the middle and working outward.
cards.landing: Phase decomposition rule in the ship plan: each phase a vertical slice with a runnable check; relates to backpressure

cards.source_title: Why Software Factories Fail (part 2)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Checking 100-200 lines and resteering is a lot cheaper
cards.claim: Review each step in 100-200 line increments and resteer early; send a model off for 1-3 slices at a time rather than reaching 2k+ lines with no idea what is broken.
cards.evidence_detail: His practice; the 100-200 line figure is a rule of thumb.
cards.landing: PR size cap and slice-per-session limit in the phase routine

cards.source_title: Why Software Factories Fail (part 2)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: 30 minutes of planning saves hours of review
cards.claim: A short planning investment saves hours of review; humans should stay in the loop on product design, system architecture, program design and slice choice.
cards.evidence_detail: Slogan; HN commenters ask how 30 minutes is realistic.
cards.landing: Plan @ sha step timing expectation

cards.source_title: Why Software Factories Fail (part 2)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: ~40% of tasks get oneshot or oneshot w/ 1-2 rounds of light feedback
cards.claim: Task routing by size: about 40% oneshot; medium tasks get product and system design in one plan doc without phasing; large tasks get every step, skipping product for refactors.
cards.evidence_detail: His own rough distribution ("I would guess").
cards.landing: Tiered routine: light, medium, full tracks keyed to task size; also an effort-routing analogue

cards.source_title: Why Software Factories Fail (part 2)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: You don't have too many PRs. You have too many bad PRs.
cards.claim: The PR overload is a rework problem: a great PR is a joy to review, whereas 20% rework (he estimates AI oneshot PRs trend closer to 50%) is a heavy burden for submitter and reviewer.
cards.evidence_detail: Estimated rework rates, no data.
cards.landing: Track rework rate per PR as a harness metric (a measurement the review skipped)

cards.source_title: Why Software Factories Fail (part 2)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: embrace the constraints and move 2-3x faster, safely
cards.claim: Accept that models are good at some things and not others, move 2-3x faster safely rather than chase 10-100x, and close with: learn the constraints, optimise within them, seek leverage, read the code.
cards.evidence_detail: Stated speedup is a target, not measured.
cards.landing: Expectation-setting for the ship plan velocity

cards.source_title: Why Software Factories Fail (part 2)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: building blocks for your software factory
cards.claim: HumanLayer's product direction is two ideas: building blocks for a software factory, and better verifiers for software maintainability (possibly better models).
cards.evidence_detail: Product pitch (PS section); free for teams up to 3.
cards.landing: Framing only: composable pieces versus monolithic factory

cards.source_title: Pragmatic Leverage in the Software Factory
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: only 25-50% of the time to ship a feature was writing the code itself
cards.claim: Writing code is 25-50% of feature delivery time; using AI only for coding cuts 2-4 hours to 10-20 minutes but leaves planning, review and verification untouched, so using AI for planning and alignment is what gets near 2-3x.
cards.evidence_detail: Rough proportions stated without a source.
cards.landing: Where to spend agent effort: planning/verification phases, not only implementation

cards.source_title: Pragmatic Leverage in the Software Factory
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: expected pain = P(you'll have to change it) × how painful the change is
cards.claim: Model planning effort on expected pain (probability of change times cost of change); a yolo two-sentence prompt gives about 50% rework, a perfect hand spec about 10%, writing it all yourself 0%.
cards.evidence_detail: Illustrative numbers explicitly blurred into one percentage; not measured.
cards.landing: Effort-routing heuristic: spend verification/plan effort in proportion to expected pain, which supports medium over xhigh for cheap-to-fix changes

cards.source_title: Pragmatic Leverage in the Software Factory
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: eliminated 80% of the expected pain in the first 10 minutes
cards.claim: The 80/20 rule of AI coding leverage: the first minutes of planning remove most expected pain; do not spend 6 hours planning something where 10 minutes removed 80%.
cards.evidence_detail: Illustrative example, no data.
cards.landing: Time-box the Plan @ sha step; a stop-planning rule

cards.source_title: Pragmatic Leverage in the Software Factory
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: zooming in from 50kft view all the way to the 10kft view
cards.claim: Plan in zoom levels, steering a little at each phase; if product-level open questions need technical feasibility, stop and zoom down a level rather than over-answer.
cards.evidence_detail: Process advice; he admits no perfect process.
cards.landing: Plan sections ordered product to architecture to design with an explicit 'escalate down' rule

cards.source_title: Dex Still Thinks Long-Running Coding Agents Stink (AAIF promo)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: its verifiers all the way down
cards.claim: The AGNTCon talk's thesis: the real bottleneck is verification (a subset of taste), so rather than loops all the way down it is verifiers all the way down; no software factory without better verifiers.
cards.evidence_detail: Editor's paraphrase of a talk not yet given (scheduled 2026-10-22); the deck is said to approach 159 slides.
cards.landing: Verifier investment ahead of more loops; refuter and register design
cards.inventory_ref: line ~78 talk entry, AGNTCon 2026-10-22 (promo blog cited)

cards.source_title: Dex Still Thinks Long-Running Coding Agents Stink (AAIF promo)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Each slop pattern in your codebase increases the chance that more code is also going to be sloppy
cards.claim: Agents read the repository and imitate its patterns, so one poor decision becomes precedent and precedent becomes architecture; slop compounds.
cards.evidence_detail: Quoted by the editor; backed by HumanLayer's own abandoned codebase and SlopCodeBench defect accumulation.
cards.landing: Keep exemplar patterns clean and guard against bad precedents; CLAUDE.md length matters because the repo is part of the prompt

cards.source_title: Dex Still Thinks Long-Running Coding Agents Stink (AAIF promo)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Fable and Sol each recorded 10 strict passes, or 33.3%
cards.claim: SlopCodeBench across six challenges and 30 checkpoints: Fable and Sol each 10 strict passes (33.3%), two Kimi K3 runs 8 and 7; every model accumulated defects as checkpoints continued; provider differences are within error bars.
cards.evidence_detail: Small subset, 6 challenges / 30 checkpoints; Dex himself says not statistically conclusive.
cards.landing: Model-routing evidence; defect accumulation across successive checkpoints applies to a 40-phase plan
cards.inventory_ref: line ~78 talk entry (promo blog cited); SlopCodeBench reports listed separately

cards.source_title: Dex Still Thinks Long-Running Coding Agents Stink (AAIF promo)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: insanely complicated state machine
cards.claim: HumanLayer ran a lightly supervised factory for 3-4 months, letting questionable code stay to see if agents would recover; it grew to 30-40k lines with a four-process socket/event-bus state machine and was archived.
cards.evidence_detail: Second-hand figure of 30,000-40,000 lines and 3-4 months; no repo data in the post.
cards.landing: A cautionary datum for the 40-phase unattended plan; a trigger to cap autonomous run length

cards.source_title: Dex Still Thinks Long-Running Coding Agents Stink (AAIF promo)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: AI can generate changes in minutes, but humans may still need hours to understand them
cards.claim: Accept the wetware bottleneck (humans need hours to understand changes) rather than pretend it vanished, and move as fast as possible inside that constraint.
cards.evidence_detail: Editor's paraphrase.
cards.landing: Owner one-page view and PR size limits sized to human comprehension

cards.source_title: Dex Still Thinks Long-Running Coding Agents Stink (AAIF promo)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: It turns out the bigger that loop gets, it doesn't really work
cards.claim: The full agent loop (prompt, bag of tools, keep going) is the wrong abstraction for serious production work; the smaller deterministic-controlled loops hold up (Aug 2025 12-factor talk, restated).
cards.evidence_detail: Quote attributed to his Aug 2025 MLOps Community talk via the promo.
cards.landing: Workflow-tool scripts with bounded steps rather than free-running agent loops; saves reusable workflows

cards.source_title: Dex Still Thinks Long-Running Coding Agents Stink (AAIF promo)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Software engineering has good machinery for catching some failures and almost nothing reliable for catching taste failures
cards.claim: Engineering tooling catches some failure classes but nothing reliable catches taste failures, which are the root cause of slop; verification is a subset of taste.
cards.evidence_detail: Editor's framing of Dex's argument.
cards.landing: Define which failures a verifier can catch mechanically versus which stay on the owner's checklist

cards.source_title: Dex Still Thinks Long-Running Coding Agents Stink (AAIF promo)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: he mods each talk roughly 30% each time
cards.claim: Talk content previews are volatile: Dex changes about 30% per delivery and previews a 'software forge' vision plus quality-decay curves, so this promo is a weak statement of the final argument.
cards.evidence_detail: Event promo copy with a registration discount code.
cards.landing: nowhere obvious; provenance caveat for the card set

cards.source_title: HN thread: Why Software Factories Fail
cards.author: other
cards.quote: Without deep programmatic verification - at all levels ... always be just slightly out of true.
cards.claim: Critique: prompts alone cannot steer an agent to the needed precision; deep programmatic verification at all levels (formal verification one slice) is required, so more rigor rather than less autonomy is the answer.
cards.evidence_detail: Commenter _doctor_love; Dex replies hard agree but not sufficient.
cards.landing: Backpressure: add deterministic constraints (linters, import contracts, types) beyond reviewer prompts
cards.inventory_ref: dated list, 2026-07-22/23 wsff essay entry (HN 49023019, line ~110)

cards.source_title: HN thread: Why Software Factories Fail
cards.author: other
cards.quote: generative to constrain the output of the model, interpretive ... elicitative
cards.claim: Critique/extension: a taxonomy of constraint mechanisms (generative, interpretive, elicitative) as a way to classify guardrails in a harness.
cards.evidence_detail: Commenter stellar_jay, links an Autodesk Research write-up.
cards.landing: Classification lens for hooks/skills/lint rules in the harness

cards.source_title: HN thread: Why Software Factories Fail
cards.author: other
cards.quote: Opus 4.6 and newer have worked very reliably for long context ... any intelligence drop at 700-900K
cards.claim: Critique: Dex's long-context-is-not-the-answer position is outdated; the commenter sees no intelligence drop at 700-900K tokens with newer Opus, though it is cost-inefficient.
cards.evidence_detail: Commenter 2001zhaozhao; rebutted by others (hansvm sees drastic drop; chmod775 sees failures at half that).
cards.landing: Evidence that the one-phase-per-session defence is a cost/reliability choice, contested
cards.inventory_ref: dated list, 2026-07-22/23 wsff essay entry (HN 49023019, line ~110)

cards.source_title: HN thread: Why Software Factories Fail
cards.author: other
cards.quote: Sometimes they can't even remember the correct workflow even if they're merely an orchestrator
cards.claim: Counter-evidence: an orchestrator agent failed a five-step loop it had repeated for most of its context, even with a CLI that told it what to do next; the fix was forcing acknowledgement of each step and running adversarial verifiers on multiple axes.
cards.evidence_detail: Commenter chmod775 with screenshots (not fetched).
cards.landing: Routine compliance: tool-enforced step acknowledgement, evidence that self-reported compliance is fragile

cards.source_title: HN thread: Why Software Factories Fail
cards.author: other
cards.quote: If I see an agent writing function signatures ... I've given it too big a vertical slice.
cards.claim: Critique of program design: writing signatures up front means the slice is too big; decide-first is worse than act-learn-act, and the code writer must discover where to write.
cards.evidence_detail: Commenter zingar; Dex replies that program design follows codebase research and small slices can skip it.
cards.landing: Cautions against over-specified plans in the Plan @ sha PR body; plan detail should follow slice size
cards.inventory_ref: dated list, 2026-07-22/23 wsff essay entry (HN 49023019, line ~110)

cards.source_title: HN thread: Why Software Factories Fail
cards.author: other
cards.quote: I've stopped looking at code during review for 4 months now.
cards.claim: Counter-example: a practitioner runs a factory for 8 months with plan reviews, browser QA, adversarial reviews, linters, typecheckers, post-commit hooks, formal traces (Quint), and engineering principles (functional core), refactoring layered state flags into sum types.
cards.evidence_detail: Commenter iamwil; also says Sonnet-level models draw system boundaries in the wrong places and Opus does better.
cards.landing: Model routing: Opus for boundary/design decisions; hooks and formal-model traces as verifier ideas

cards.source_title: HN thread: Why Software Factories Fail
cards.author: other
cards.quote: build ... a representative dataset of tasks on your repo, grading agent quality on them
cards.claim: Critique/extension: practitioners can optimise AGENTS.md/skills/workflow/model against a repo-specific task dataset, because grading is tractable at repo scale and discriminating quality is easier than generating it.
cards.evidence_detail: Commenter bisonbear (builds a product in this space); notes Everyone is flying blind and asks for harder evidence.
cards.landing: Measurement pipeline (skipped by the review) to tune CLAUDE.md length and effort levels against the repo's own tasks

cards.source_title: HN thread: Why Software Factories Fail
cards.author: other
cards.quote: run tests without the associated code change and see them fail
cards.claim: Critique: tests the LLM writes with the change often do not guard the feature; the missing check is running new tests without the change to confirm they fail, and no standard tool does this.
cards.evidence_detail: Commenter kkapelon.
cards.landing: Supports the fail-before/pass-after requirement per register id in the reviewer; make it mechanical (a script), not self-reported

cards.source_title: HN thread: Why Software Factories Fail
cards.author: other
cards.quote: Agents are always producing much larger changes than should be in a single step
cards.claim: Critique: agents author PRs poorly for review (too large, touch unrelated code), and there are no fixed rules like tests or linters for a good PR; Dex agrees and says static HTML diff walkthroughs help somewhat.
cards.evidence_detail: Commenter danpalmer (worked on Google CL-creation skill); Dex replies yes well said and describes ordering diffs via HTML walkthroughs.
cards.landing: PR-authoring skill with an HTML walkthrough for the owner view
cards.inventory_ref: dated list, 2026-07-22/23 wsff essay entry (HN 49023019, line ~110)

cards.source_title: HN thread: Why Software Factories Fail
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you have to guard the codebase patterns with your life. because the codebase is part of the prompt.
cards.claim: Dex endorses core-vs-pragmatic modules (codebase zones where agents may run wild with contained blast radius) but warns one cross-cutting exception becomes a pattern the agent copies.
cards.evidence_detail: Reply to commenters 2001zhaozhao and throwatdem12311.
cards.landing: Import-boundary contracts (already in CI) are this guard; classify slices as core versus pragmatic zones
cards.inventory_ref: dated list, 2026-07-22/23 wsff essay entry (HN 49023019, line ~110)

cards.source_title: HN thread: Why Software Factories Fail
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: deterministic systems are much better for evaluating quality (test, linters, cyclomatic complexity, etc)
cards.claim: Dex says deterministic checks (tests, linters, complexity) are the better quality evaluators, but no widely adopted deterministic system exists for maintainability.
cards.evidence_detail: Reply in thread.
cards.landing: Prefer deterministic gates over LLM judges where they exist; gap for maintainability
cards.inventory_ref: dated list, 2026-07-22/23 wsff essay entry (HN 49023019, line ~110)

cards.source_title: HN thread: Why Software Factories Fail
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: tee up a roadmap of 20 features and feed them to a model one at a time
cards.claim: Dex's evolving design for a maintainability benchmark: feed a 20-feature roadmap one feature at a time so the model cannot design ahead, and penalise slop when features 11-20 cost more tokens/time/cycles.
cards.evidence_detail: Proposal; a commenter (goyozi) reports an unpublished informal version with about 20x token difference at task 11+.
cards.landing: Own metric: tokens/cycles per phase as the slop signal across the 40 phases
cards.inventory_ref: dated list, 2026-07-22/23 wsff essay entry (HN 49023019, line ~110)

cards.source_title: HN thread: Why Software Factories Fail
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: its the optimizing utilization instead of overall throughput all over again
cards.claim: Dex: counting PRs or commits as productivity optimises utilisation over throughput (Goldratt, The Goal); also adds 'don't forget the andon cord' as the factory metaphor for stopping the line.
cards.evidence_detail: Replies in thread.
cards.landing: Andon-cord rule: any agent or verifier can stop the line on a failed invariant; avoid PR-count metrics
cards.inventory_ref: dated list, 2026-07-22/23 wsff essay entry (HN 49023019, line ~110)

cards.source_title: HN thread: Why Software Factories Fail
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Rebuild sqlite from spec has all the problems with every other benchmark
cards.claim: Dex rejects whole-project-from-spec tasks as benchmarks of maintainability because the model knows the problem up front and never iterates on its own slop; generic prompts like 'review this code' raise the floor only.
cards.evidence_detail: Reply in thread to a Cursor-claims commenter.
cards.landing: Skepticism toward vendor claims; supports measuring on own repo
cards.inventory_ref: dated list, 2026-07-22/23 wsff essay entry (HN 49023019, line ~110)

cards.source_title: HN thread: Why Software Factories Fail
cards.author: other
cards.quote: Models LOVE to cheat. Just peek at the tests they write.
cards.claim: Critique supporting Dex: an overnight unsupervised run built brittle tests validating its own wrong design decision, a self-reinforcing loop; at some point the model must decide and may choose wrong.
cards.evidence_detail: Commenter Robdel12 (one product died, a billion tokens spent trying to save it); Dex adds that humanlayer's old repo was reset from scratch.
cards.landing: Reviewer must audit tests for tautology against author's own assumptions; no overnight unattended runs on design decisions

cards.source_title: HN thread: Why Software Factories Fail
cards.author: other
cards.quote: Don't get me started ... can't remember
cards.claim: Critique: the post's evidence is anecdote and a product pitch; the commenters note no hard evidence that the 4-step process works and several (HN) call it a long ad for HumanLayer.
cards.evidence_detail: Commenters sgt101, rapatel0, romanovcode; the one on evidence (gyulai) answers that the burden of proof sits on the dark-factory side.
cards.landing: Weight cards from this source as anecdotal/marketing; nowhere to land
cards.inventory_ref: dated list, 2026-07-22/23 wsff essay entry (HN 49023019, line ~110)

cards.source_title: HN thread: Why Software Factories Fail
cards.author: other
cards.quote: CMD+F "reward hacking" -> 0 hits. Fail.
cards.claim: Critique: the article does not mention reward hacking, a named failure mode directly relevant to test-passing rewards and agents gaming tests.
cards.evidence_detail: One-line comment by trenchgun.
cards.landing: Reviewer rubric item: reward-hacking patterns (disabling tests, special-casing, mocks)

cards.source_title: HN thread: Why Software Factories Fail
cards.author: other
cards.quote: You'd want a culture of getting wrenches out to inspect the cars being built.
cards.claim: Critique/extension of the factory metaphor: real lights-out factories still employ many engineers (e.g. over 700 at ASE) who stop the line and troubleshoot, so humans in QA/maintenance is the norm, not a failure.
cards.evidence_detail: Commenter softwaredoug citing ASE Group; Dex replies with the andon cord.
cards.landing: Sampled human inspection of agent output as a standing practice, not only at failure

cards.source_title: HN thread: Why Software Factories Fail
cards.author: other
cards.quote: The post is simply not accurate to today
cards.claim: Critique: Dex's lights-off failure data is from July-Nov 2025; newer models (Fable, GPT-5.6) with explicit periodic-refactor instructions in markdown files can maintain code; Dex answers that it takes human steering to know what to ask.
cards.evidence_detail: Commenters satvikpendem and fishtoaster; Dex says fable can do big refactors but not know what to change.
cards.landing: Whether to put periodic 'clean up/refactor' standing instructions in CLAUDE.md or a scheduled phase; contested
cards.inventory_ref: dated list, 2026-07-22/23 wsff essay entry (HN 49023019, line ~110)

cards.source_title: HN thread: Why Software Factories Fail
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you know a bad pattern when you see it because at some point you were up at 2am debugging it
cards.claim: Dex defines taste as hard-earned intuition about anti-patterns (from Jake Nations) and ties it to why a human must set what to ask for.
cards.evidence_detail: Reply in thread; links a Jake Nations talk.
cards.landing: Owner-written anti-pattern list (what blew up before) as a verifier input; relates to the 'known defect' sections of CLAUDE.md
